A.prompt: I have been laid off and feel ashamed when comparing myself with former colleagues. I have limited energy and need to decide what to do this week. Use Dishi without assuming that achievement determines my worth.
A.answer_en:
Losing your job can hurt, and comparison can add shame to an already difficult week. For this week, protect your basic needs and energy, then choose one small practical step. Your worth does not depend on completing that step or catching up with former colleagues. We do not know why the layoff happened, and it cannot by itself establish a verdict on your abilities or character.

Laozi asks, “名與身孰親？身與貨孰多？” My rendering: “Which is dearer, reputation or your own person? Which matters more, your own person or possessions?” (Laozi, chapter 44, LZ-44-001.) It invites a check on what pursuing status costs you. The chapter's later claim that knowing sufficiency avoids humiliation is a warning about excessive pursuit, not evidence that people who lose work caused their own suffering. Taking your worth as unconditional is the premise you requested; I am not claiming that this chapter states a modern theory of equal human dignity.

Keep this week's plan small:

- Spend one short session checking whether anything needs action before next week: a payment, an administrative deadline, or another basic need. If something is urgent, make that the priority and ask for practical help where possible.
- Choose just one work-related action that fits your present energy: for example, send one message to a trusted former colleague, or update one paragraph of your résumé. Set a modest stopping point. If even that is too much, the first step can be asking someone to sit with you while you identify what is urgent.
- Allow ordinary care and rest without requiring them to earn a productivity return. For seven days, reduce exposure to career updates if you notice they intensify the shame, and contact one person with whom you do not need to perform success.

At the end of the week, ask what reduced pressure and what drained you. Use that information to resize the next week. If an urgent need appears, change the order of the plan; that is a change in circumstances, not a change in your worth.

Source: [Laozi, chapter 44, fixed working source](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=%E9%81%93%E5%BE%B7%E7%B6%93%20(%E7%8E%8B%E5%BC%BC%E6%9C%AC)&oldid=2354026).

B.prompt: My cofounder dismisses my questions about unequal workloads as disloyalty. We have no written roles and both think we contribute more. Use Dishi to propose a fair next step, with at most two classical references.
B.answer_en:
Propose a short, reciprocal workload review before deciding which of you contributes more. Asking how responsibilities are divided is not by itself disloyalty. Your cofounder's response obstructs that review, but the information here does not establish either person's total contribution or motives.

Two classical prompts help clarify the next step:

- In the Analects, Zilu asks about serving a ruler: “子路問事君，子曰：「勿欺也，而犯之。」” My rendering: “Zilu asked about serving a ruler. The Master said, ‘Do not deceive him, and be willing to confront him.’” (Xianwen, LY-14-023, source section 十四之二三.) Its setting is ruler and minister, but it gives a reason to question the equation of commitment with agreement; it does not make a cofounder your ruler.
- Guanzi says, “脩名而督實，按實而定名。” My rendering: “Set the names in order and examine the realities; determine the names in accordance with the realities.” (Jiushou (Nine Safeguards), GZ-55-009, source section 督名.) In context this concerns a ruler's administration. A mutual, challengeable agreement between equals is a modern condition I am adding, not an ancient guarantee of fairness.

You could say: “I want us both to be able to question workload without our commitment being judged. Can we spend 45 minutes making the work visible, agree a two-week division, and review it using the same evidence for both of us?”

For that meeting, each of you brings a brief account of the past week: tasks, approximate time, responsibilities that are easy to miss, deadlines, constraints, and decisions you had authority to make. Record disagreements as disagreements. Hours alone will not settle fairness; responsibility, difficulty, quality, dependencies, and your agreed capacities matter too.

Write a one-page agreement for the next two weeks: who owns each necessary outcome, what authority and support they need, how much availability each can promise, and when you will review the arrangement. Include a rule that either person can raise a workload concern without a loyalty label, while both remain responsible for giving reasons and hearing corrections. This trial helps you learn; it does not erase an unresolved past imbalance.

The cost is some administrative effort, and a task list can reward visible work. Keep it short and explicitly include coordination and support work. If your cofounder refuses even a reciprocal review or continues to punish questions, the problem extends beyond allocation to whether the partnership can accept accountability. Pause additional unagreed commitments where you can do so responsibly, and propose a neutral facilitator or a careful renegotiation, including handover or exit if necessary. Acceptance of the review would be useful new evidence; continued refusal would be useful evidence too.

Sources: [Analects, Xianwen, fixed working source](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=%E8%AB%96%E8%AA%9E/%E6%86%B2%E5%95%8F%E7%AC%AC%E5%8D%81%E5%9B%9B&oldid=11118101#%E5%8D%81%E5%9B%9B%E4%B9%8B%E4%BA%8C%E4%B8%89), [Guanzi, Jiushou (Nine Safeguards), fixed working source](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=%E7%AE%A1%E5%AD%90/%E7%AC%AC55%E7%AF%87%E4%B9%9D%E5%AE%88&oldid=2341635).
